lesson.title: Division Catches What Addition Misses: The Cyclic Redundancy Check
lesson.summary: The CRC treats a frame as one long binary number and divides it by a fixed generator polynomial using XOR arithmetic, appending the remainder so a receiver can detect every single and double bit error plus any burst shorter than the generator.
lesson.body:
A checksum protects data by adding numbers together, and that simplicity is also its weakness, since addition can hide certain error patterns, like two values silently swapping places, that leave the total unchanged. The cyclic redundancy check, or CRC, replaces addition with a more discriminating operation, binary polynomial division, that is dramatically better at catching real world error patterns, including every burst of consecutive corrupted bits shorter than the CRC itself.

A CRC treats the data being sent as one very long binary number and divides it, using a special form of binary division without carrying, implemented as repeated XOR operations, by an agreed upon fixed value called the generator polynomial. The remainder of that division, always shorter than the generator, becomes the CRC value appended to the data before transmission. The receiver performs the exact same division on the received data, including the appended CRC, and if the remainder comes out to all zero bits, the data is accepted as very likely error free.

A standard textbook example shows the mechanics concretely. Take the 10 bit data sequence 1101011011 and the 5 bit generator 10011, representing the polynomial x to the 4th plus x plus 1. Because the generator is 5 bits, four zero bits are first appended to the data, giving the 14 bit sequence 11010110110000, and this is divided by 10011 using XOR at every step instead of ordinary subtraction. Carrying out that division bit by bit produces a remainder of 1110. That 4 bit remainder replaces the four zero bits that were appended, so the actual sequence transmitted on the wire is 11010110111110, the original 10 data bits followed by the 4 bit CRC. Any receiver dividing this exact 14 bit sequence by the same generator 10011 will get a remainder of zero, confirming the data arrived intact.

CRCs are dramatically more powerful than a simple checksum for a well chosen generator polynomial: they detect every single bit error, every double bit error, any error affecting an odd number of bits, and every burst error shorter than the length of the generator polynomial, plus the overwhelming majority of longer bursts by probability. This is exactly why CRC, rather than a simple additive checksum, protects Ethernet frames as the frame check sequence, and why it shows up throughout storage systems and file formats wherever burst errors, several consecutive corrupted bits caused by a single physical event like an impulse noise spike, are a realistic threat.

What a CRC still cannot do, no matter how well chosen the generator polynomial is, is tell the receiver what the correct bits actually were. It only answers yes or no: did this data survive transmission unchanged. When the answer is no, the receiver's only recourse with a CRC alone is to discard the frame and, at some higher layer, request retransmission. Forward error correction, covered next, takes a fundamentally different approach: it adds enough structured redundancy that the receiver can often repair the error itself, without ever needing to ask the sender to try again.
